{{Short description|Open-source 3D-printed microscope}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=October 2026}}
The '''OpenFlexure Microscope''' is an [[open-source hardware|open-source]], [[3D printing|3D-printed]] laboratory [[microscope]] with motorised sample positioning and focus control.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Collins |first1=Joel T. |display-authors=etal |title=Robotic microscopy for everyone: the OpenFlexure microscope |journal=[[Biomedical Optics Express]] |date=8 April 2020 |volume=11 |issue=5 |pages=2447–2460 |doi=10.1364/BOE.385729 |pmc=7249832 |pmid=32499936 |quote=Here we present an open-source, 3D-printed, and fully-automated laboratory microscope, with motorised sample positioning and focus control.}}</ref> It uses a mechanical stage built from plastic [[Compliant mechanism|flexures]] and is designed so that it can be manufactured and maintained locally.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Collins |first1=Joel T. |display-authors=etal |title=Robotic microscopy for everyone: the OpenFlexure microscope |journal=[[Biomedical Optics Express]] |date=8 April 2020 |volume=11 |issue=5 |pages=2447–2460 |doi=10.1364/BOE.385729 |pmc=7249832 |pmid=32499936 |quote=The OpenFlexure microscope has been designed to enable low-volume manufacturing and maintenance by local personnel, vastly increasing accessibility.}}</ref>

== History ==
A one-piece 3D-printed flexure translation stage for microscopy was described in 2016 by J. P. Sharkey, D. C. W. Foo, A. Kabla, J. J. Baumberg and R. W. Bowman.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Collins |first1=Joel T. |display-authors=etal |title=Robotic microscopy for everyone: the OpenFlexure microscope |journal=[[Biomedical Optics Express]] |date=8 April 2020 |volume=11 |issue=5 |pages=2447–2460 |doi=10.1364/BOE.385729 |pmc=7249832 |pmid=32499936 |quote=Sharkey J. P., Foo D. C., Kabla A., Baumberg J. J., Bowman R. W., “A one-piece 3D printed flexure translation stage for open-source microscopy,” Rev. Sci. Instrum. 87(2), 025104 (2016).}}</ref> The microscope itself was presented in a 2020 paper in ''[[Biomedical Optics Express]]'' by a team at the University of Bath with partners in Tanzania, including the [[Ifakara Health Institute]] and STICLab in [[Dar es Salaam]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Collins |first1=Joel T. |display-authors=etal |title=Robotic microscopy for everyone: the OpenFlexure microscope |journal=[[Biomedical Optics Express]] |date=8 April 2020 |volume=11 |issue=5 |pages=2447–2460 |doi=10.1364/BOE.385729 |pmc=7249832 |pmid=32499936 |quote=Centre for Photonics and Photonic Materials, Department of Physics, University of Bath, UK 2 Ifakara Health Institute, Ifakara, Tanzania 3 STICLab, Dar Es Salaam, Tanzania}}</ref> The paper was received on 12 December 2019 and published on 8 April 2020.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Collins |first1=Joel T. |display-authors=etal |title=Robotic microscopy for everyone: the OpenFlexure microscope |journal=[[Biomedical Optics Express]] |date=8 April 2020 |volume=11 |issue=5 |pages=2447–2460 |doi=10.1364/BOE.385729 |pmc=7249832 |pmid=32499936 |quote=Received 2019 Dec 12; Revised 2020 Mar 6; Accepted 2020 Mar 9}}</ref>

The project's website says it was "once based primarily at the University of Bath and University of Cambridge" and has since spread, and that the core development team is now at the [[University of Glasgow]].<ref>{{cite web |title=About the OpenFlexure Project |url=https://openflexure.org/about/ |website=OpenFlexure |access-date=3 October 2026 |quote=Once based primarily at the University of Bath and University of Cambridge, the project has spread. [...] As an academic project, the core development team is now based at the University of Glasgow.}}</ref> It also says the microscope is used in over 50 countries.<ref>{{cite web |title=About the OpenFlexure Project |url=https://openflexure.org/about/ |website=OpenFlexure |access-date=3 October 2026 |quote=Used in over 50 countries and every continent, the project aims to enable Microscopy for Everyone .}}</ref>

== Design ==
=== Hardware ===
The positioning mechanism is a flexure design that gives 3-axis motion, with step sizes as low as 50 nm along the z axis and 70 nm along x and y, and a travel of 12 × 12 × 4 mm.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Collins |first1=Joel T. |display-authors=etal |title=Robotic microscopy for everyone: the OpenFlexure microscope |journal=[[Biomedical Optics Express]] |date=8 April 2020 |volume=11 |issue=5 |pages=2447–2460 |doi=10.1364/BOE.385729 |pmc=7249832 |pmid=32499936 |quote=This mechanism provides 3-axis positioning with step sizes as low as 50 nm in the z axis, and 70 nm in x and y . The range of mechanical motion is smaller than traditional mechanical stages, with 12 × 12 × 4 mm travel}}</ref> Because the stage uses plastic flexures, the project says its motion is "free from friction and vibration", and most of the microscope, including all the parts with flexures, prints as a single piece.<ref>{{cite web |title=Introduction to the OpenFlexure Microscope |url=https://openflexure.org/projects/microscope/ |website=OpenFlexure |access-date=3 October 2026 |quote=This design for a 3D printed microscope stage uses plastic flexures, meaning its motion is free from friction and vibration. [...] most of the microscope (including all the parts with flexures) prints as a single piece.}}</ref> The microscope fits within 15 × 15 × 20 cm and weighs about 500 g in its highest-resolution, fully automated configuration.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Collins |first1=Joel T. |display-authors=etal |title=Robotic microscopy for everyone: the OpenFlexure microscope |journal=[[Biomedical Optics Express]] |date=8 April 2020 |volume=11 |issue=5 |pages=2447–2460 |doi=10.1364/BOE.385729 |pmc=7249832 |pmid=32499936 |quote=The microscope is both compact, fitting within a 15 cm × 15 cm × 20 cm volume, and lightweight at ≈ 500 g in its highest resolution, fully automated configuration.}}</ref> The plastic construction limits its load capacity, so it is not suited to very large or heavy samples.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Collins |first1=Joel T. |display-authors=etal |title=Robotic microscopy for everyone: the OpenFlexure microscope |journal=[[Biomedical Optics Express]] |date=8 April 2020 |volume=11 |issue=5 |pages=2447–2460 |doi=10.1364/BOE.385729 |pmc=7249832 |pmid=32499936 |quote=due to the primarily plastic construction, our design has a limited load capacity unsuitable for very large or heavy samples}}</ref>

The optics can be changed. According to the project, they range "from a webcam lens to a 100x, oil immersion objective".<ref>{{cite web |title=OpenFlexure Microscope README |url=https://gitlab.com/openflexure/openflexure-microscope/-/blob/master/README.md |website=GitLab |publisher=OpenFlexure |access-date=3 October 2026 |quote=There are many different options for the optics, ranging from a webcam lens to a 100x, oil immersion objective.}}</ref> The authors list options including transmission and reflection illumination, polarisation contrast and epi-fluorescence imaging.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Collins |first1=Joel T. |display-authors=etal |title=Robotic microscopy for everyone: the OpenFlexure microscope |journal=[[Biomedical Optics Express]] |date=8 April 2020 |volume=11 |issue=5 |pages=2447–2460 |doi=10.1364/BOE.385729 |pmc=7249832 |pmid=32499936 |quote=The microscope is highly customisable, with a number of options readily available including trans- and epi- illumination, polarisation contrast imaging, and epi-florescence [sic] imaging.}}</ref>

In an appendix the authors estimate the cost of the lowest-cost version, which has no motors, a webcam for sensor and optics, and no microcomputer: about US$5 of [[polylactic acid|PLA]], about US$5 for the webcam, and common hardware at about US$5 if bought in bulk or about US$26 if bought in single packs. The estimate excludes the 3D printer.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Collins |first1=Joel T. |display-authors=etal |title=Robotic microscopy for everyone: the OpenFlexure microscope |journal=[[Biomedical Optics Express]] |date=8 April 2020 |volume=11 |issue=5 |pages=2447–2460 |doi=10.1364/BOE.385729 |pmc=7249832 |pmid=32499936 |quote=Low-cost version No motors, cheap webcam as sensor and optics, no microcomputer. • PLA: ≈ $ 5 USD. • Low-cost webcam: ≈ $ 5 USD. • Common hardware: Bulk ≈ $ 5 USD, one-off ≈ $ 26 USD (see Table 1 ) [...] Likewise, the cost of 3D printers themselves are excluded.}}</ref>

=== Variants ===
The '''OpenFlexure Delta Stage''' is a separate 3D-printed design "designed for researchers" that is controlled by the same software, and has been used for imaging modes including brightfield, epi-fluorescence, darkfield, Rheinberg and differential phase contrast.<ref>{{cite arXiv |last1=McDermott |first1=Samuel |last2=Ayazi |first2=Filip |last3=Collins |first3=Joel |last4=Knapper |first4=Joe |last5=Stirling |first5=Julian |last6=Bowman |first6=Richard |last7=Cicuta |first7=Pietro |title=Multi-modal microscopy imaging with the OpenFlexure Delta Stage |eprint=2112.05804 |date=2021 |quote=Here we present the OpenFlexure Delta Stage, a 3D-printed microscope designed for researchers. Powered by the OpenFlexure software stack, it is capable of performing automated experiments.}}</ref>

=== Software ===
The control software is split into client and server applications that communicate through a web API conforming to the [[World Wide Web Consortium|W3C]] [[Web of Things]] standard.<ref>{{cite arXiv |last1=Collins |first1=Joel T. |last2=Knapper |first2=Joe |last3=Stirling |first3=Julian |last4=McDermott |first4=Samuel |last5=Bowman |first5=Richard |title=Modern Microscopy with the Web of Things: The OpenFlexure Microscope Software Stack |eprint=2101.00933 |class=physics.ins-det |date=2021 |quote=We split the control code into client and server applications interfaced via a web API that conforms to the W3C Web of Things standard. This enables simple control of the microscope from multiple languages, provides a modern graphical control interface, and minimises duplicated code.}}</ref> The server is described by its developers as an "API server and web interface for the OpenFlexure Microscope".<ref>{{cite web |title=openflexure-microscope-server |url=https://gitlab.com/openflexure/openflexure-microscope-server |website=GitLab |publisher=OpenFlexure |access-date=3 October 2026 |quote=API server and web interface for the OpenFlexure Microscope.}}</ref>

== Local production ==
The authors report that they produced "over 100 microscopes in Tanzania and Kenya for educational, scientific, and clinical applications".<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Collins |first1=Joel T. |display-authors=etal |title=Robotic microscopy for everyone: the OpenFlexure microscope |journal=[[Biomedical Optics Express]] |date=8 April 2020 |volume=11 |issue=5 |pages=2447–2460 |doi=10.1364/BOE.385729 |pmc=7249832 |pmid=32499936 |quote=We have produced over 100 microscopes in Tanzania and Kenya for educational, scientific, and clinical applications}}</ref> The paper names STICLab's facility in Dar es Salaam and the partner Tech for Trade in [[Nairobi]] as production sites, and says the designs had also been replicated in maker spaces and academic labs in Peru, Germany, Ghana, the United States and the United Kingdom.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Collins |first1=Joel T. |display-authors=etal |title=Robotic microscopy for everyone: the OpenFlexure microscope |journal=[[Biomedical Optics Express]] |date=8 April 2020 |volume=11 |issue=5 |pages=2447–2460 |doi=10.1364/BOE.385729 |pmc=7249832 |pmid=32499936 |quote=We have demonstrated the local production of microscopes for educational, scientific, and clinical applications at STICLab’s facility in Dar es Salaam, and with our partners at Tech for Trade (Nairobi, Kenya). [...] The open-source [ 33 ] designs have been replicated in maker spaces and academic labs in numerous countries including in Peru, Germany, Ghana, the USA, and the UK.}}</ref>

== Licensing ==
The hardware design is released under the CERN Open Hardware Licence version 2, strongly reciprocal (CERN-OHL-S-2.0).<ref>{{cite web |title=OpenFlexure Microscope README |url=https://gitlab.com/openflexure/openflexure-microscope/-/blob/master/README.md |website=GitLab |publisher=OpenFlexure |access-date=3 October 2026 |quote=This project is open-source and is Released under the CERN Open Hardware License, strongly reciprocal, v2.0 or later (CERN-OHL-S-2.0)}}</ref> The server software is licensed under the [[GNU General Public License]] version 3.<ref>{{cite web |title=LICENSE |url=https://gitlab.com/openflexure/openflexure-microscope-server/-/blob/master/LICENSE |website=GitLab |publisher=OpenFlexure |access-date=3 October 2026 |quote=GNU GENERAL PUBLIC LICENSE Version 3, 29 June 2007}}</ref> The project does not sell microscopes itself, but several companies do.<ref>{{cite web |title=OpenFlexure Microscope README |url=https://gitlab.com/openflexure/openflexure-microscope/-/blob/master/README.md |website=GitLab |publisher=OpenFlexure |access-date=3 October 2026 |quote=The OpenFlexure Project doesn't sell micrscopes [sic], but several companies do}}</ref>
